newsitem.title: ICELAND: FEATURE - Fish inflame northern passions.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fish inflame northern passions.

text.p: The Icelandic herring boat Sigurdur VE sailed into its home port to a hero's welcome this month after being released from arrest by the Norwegian coast guard for alleged breaches of fishing regulations.

Norway has become public enemy number one in Iceland after seizing the boat, confiscating its catch of herring, and fining it and its owners 405,000 Norwegian crowns ($55,800) for not using a Norwegian catch logbook and failing to report its location.
Icelandic officials angrily reject the allegations and the tiny North Atlantic country is once again pulling the diplomatic weapons out of its armoury to protect its fisheries revenue.
Nothing is more guaranteed to make Icelandic tempers flare than a good fishing dispute with its big brothers in the North Atlantic, and with sound economic reason.
Around three-quarters of the volcanic island's export revenue and more than half of its foreign currency earnings derive from fish.
"There didn't seem to be any argument strong enough to convince the Norwegians of our innocence," skipper Kristbjoern Arnason said after weighing anchor in his home port of the Westman Islands.

Norwegian coastguards had towed his vessel to the northern port of Bodoe to make him atone for his alleged transgression. The Icelanders refused to pay the fine and the matter will come up in a Bodoe court on September 2.
THE INCIDENT BECOMES A DIPLOMATIC DISPUTE
While Norwegian officials dismissed the arrest and fining of the herring boat as a local police matter, Iceland was treating it as a political act at the very highest level.
The Icelandic ambassador to Norway, on holiday at home when the dispute broke, extended his break for a week after Reykjavik submitted a formal protest to Oslo.
A decline in the cod catch late in the 1980s plunged Iceland's economy into a deep recession from which it has only just recovered.

Questions of pure economic survival have prompted Iceland to declare successive extensions to its fishing limits, where British and other ships had been fishing cod, right up to the shore, since the year 1400.
To counter overfishing by high-powered foreign vessels, Iceland extended its fishery limits from three miles to four miles in 1952, to 12 miles in 1958, 50 miles in 1972 and 200 miles in 1975.
Britain retaliated first with a ban on imports of fish from Iceland, then by sending in Royal Navy gunboats to prevent its trawlers from being arrested, sparking the first "Cod War."

Disputes intensified, and Iceland, which has no army of its own, produced a "secret weapon" - primitive clippers used to cut the trawls from offending ships, now proudly on display at the national museum in Reykjavik.
Britain's reply was to ram the tiny coastguard boats with huge frigates.
At the height of the fourth and final Cod War, Iceland cut off diplomatic relations with fellow NATO member Britain.
Ironically, it was Norway which brought the two sides together for an agreement reached in 1976, whereby London recognized Iceland's 200-mile limit.
Britain had little choice, since by that time it was claiming a similar limit of its own, like the rest of the then-European Community.

Meanwhile, Iceland's expanding fleet began to overfish its own waters. Quotas were introduced, and faced with less fish to catch at home, Icelandic vessels began to look beyond the 200-mile limit to international waters.
ICELAND LOOKS BEYOND ITS IMPOSED LIMIT

Among the targets have been the Barents Sea loophole, a "no man's sea" between the Norwegian and Russian fishing zones far into the Arctic, and an area around Spitzbergen where Norway has declared a "fisheries protection zone."
Iceland was not satisfied with Norway's official reply on June 11, which said the Oslo government could not interfere with legal proceedings.
Norway at the same time reached out a hand of conciliation, proposing to strengthen fisheries cooperation to avoid a repetition of the Sigurdur incident.
But Icelandic Foreign Minister Halldor Asgrimsson demanded nothing less than a public apology from the Norwegian government for the seizure of the boat.

And Prime Minister David Oddsson made a sharp jab at Norway's courtship of Brussels when he commented: "If Norway had shown Iceland one percent of the submissiveness it has always shown towards the European Union, none of these disputes would ever have happened."
Norway, which like Iceland is not a member of the EU, has been lobbying hard for its fishing interests.
But while Norway has abundant offshore oil and gas, Iceland is heavily dependent on fisheries.
HERRING AND CAPELIN SET TO CAUSE TROUBLE

Cod is the main fish species at stake in the disputed zones. Another area of contention is the Herring Loophole, in the area where herring migrates westwards out of Norway's 200-mile limit, before it reaches Iceland's limit.
Herring has begun crossing from Norway to Iceland again after keeping out of Icelandic waters for 30 years. It was this stock that the boat was chasing at the time of its seizure.
The next round in the bout of the boats will be around Jan Mayen Island again this summer, when the capelin season starts, and this time Iceland will be calling the shots.
Capelin, a tiny fish used for margarine production, clearly has not read the rule book.
It migrates where the fishing zones of Greenland, Jan Mayen (Norway) and Iceland overlap, blissfully unaware of the tidal waves it is causing.
